prime.problem: Almost every tree question is a walk: print sorted keys, compute something from children, read row by row. Without a clear model of when a node is visited, you mix up the orders, and recursion on a deep tree crashes Python at about 1,000 levels.
prime.fits: The first card of Trees and heaps. It uses the parsing card's stack (DFS is a stack, explicit or the call stack) and the toolkit's deque (level order is BFS). The heap, Fenwick and segment-tree cards that follow are trees stored in arrays, walked with the same ideas.
expect: pre-, in-, post- and level order
the three visits of a depth-first walk
postorder for values computed from children (Maximum Path Sum)
recursion depth vs an explicit stack
prime.goal: Produce any of the four orders on sight, walk a tree inorder in O(1) extra space with Morris threading, and compute Maximum Path Sum with an iterative postorder.

attend: What single choice distinguishes pre-, in- and postorder?
Why is the inorder of a binary search tree sorted?
What does a Morris thread remember that a stack otherwise would?
How does Morris know whether it is visiting a node for the first or the second time?
Why does Maximum Path Sum need postorder, and why does it pass up only one arm?

must: A depth-first walk passes each node three times (down, between children, up) → writing the value at the first, second or third pass gives pre-, in- or postorder → level order is different: a FIFO queue reads row by row

A stack (or recursion) exists only to remember where to go back up → Morris stores that in the predecessor's empty right pointer (n + 1 of them exist) → first visit lays the thread, second visit finds it and removes it → O(1) extra space, tree restored

A value that depends on both children (best path bending here) must wait until both are done → postorder → through(v) = x + max(0, gL) + max(0, gR), but only x + max(0, gL, gR) can be passed up, since a path can bend only once
Recursion depth = tree height → a 1,000-node chain exceeds Python's default limit and raises RecursionError → an explicit stack costs O(h) memory but no crash; Morris costs O(1)
elevated: Morris writes into the tree while reading it → concurrent readers see threads as real edges, and stopping early leaves threads behind → use it only when asked for O(1) space on a tree you own
max(0, …) drops negative arms → a negative subtree never helps a path → best must start at −∞, not 0, or an all-negative tree returns 0
reference: build() from a level-order list with None gaps
preorder Morris as the same loop with a different write point
18 at peak stack depth for a random 1,000-node tree

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the 7-node BST (4; 2, 6; 1, 3, 5, 7), write its four orders, then explain Morris threading in 3 sentences: what a thread is, when it is laid and when removed.
checklist: orders differ only in which of the three passes writes the value
a thread points the inorder predecessor's empty right pointer back at the node
first visit lays it and goes left; second visit (thread found) removes it, writes, goes right
O(1) extra space and the tree is unchanged at the end

retrieve.q: Explain why postorder, not preorder, is the right order for Maximum Path Sum.
answer: each node needs its children's best downward gains
those exist only after both subtrees are finished
postorder visits a node after both children; preorder visits it before

retrieve.q: Walk through Morris at node 4 in the 5-node tree (4 with left subtree 2 → 1, 3 and right child 5), on both visits.
answer: first visit: walk to the predecessor, 2 → 3 (rightmost of the left subtree)
3.right is empty: lay thread 3 → 4 and go left
later, following 3's thread returns to 4; the predecessor now points to 4
second visit: remove the thread, write 4, go right to 5

retrieve.q: Recursion, explicit stack or Morris for an inorder walk of a tree that may be a 10⁵-long chain. Pick one and justify it, naming the cost of each.
answer: recursion: shortest, but RecursionError past about 1,000 levels
explicit stack: safe, O(h) memory, up to 10⁵ entries on a chain
Morris: O(1) memory, more pointer steps, writes into the tree
explicit stack unless memory is the stated constraint and the tree isn't shared

compare.q: A binary tree of node objects vs a heap stored in a list: how does each find a child, what shape does each guarantee, and which walks does each support?
answer: tree: pointers left/right; any shape, possibly a chain
heap: index arithmetic 2i + 1, 2i + 2; always complete, so depth ⌊log₂ n⌋
trees support all four orders and BST search
a heap supports only top access and root-to-leaf sifts; its order is loose, not sorted

compare.q: Tree DFS vs graph DFS: what extra state does a graph need, and why doesn't a tree?
answer: a tree has no cycles and one path to each node, so a walk never revisits
a graph can reach a node by several paths or cycles, so it needs a visited set
both use a stack (explicit or call stack), with the same recursion-depth risk

predict.q: Run Morris inorder on a 1,000-node chain where every node has only a right child. Before counting: how many threads are laid, and how many pointer moves and predecessor steps happen, compared with the card's left-leaning chain (1,999 + 1,998)?
predict.answer: No threads at all: no node has a left child, so every step takes the no-left branch, writes the value and moves right. That is 1,000 moves and 0 predecessor steps. The left-leaning chain is Morris's worst shape because every node has a left subtree whose right spine must be walked twice.

apply.done: Your trace has 10 steps with threads 3 → 4, 1 → 2 and 5 → 6 laid and removed, output 1 through 7, and totals of 10 moves and 8 predecessor steps.
